query: What compute, model-size, random-seed, and experiment-tracking budgets are required to reproducibly train and search hyperparameters for the proposed hybrid SSL+handcrafted pipeline?

response.query: What compute, model-size, random-seed, and experiment-tracking budgets are required to reproducibly train and search hyperparameters for the proposed hybrid SSL+handcrafted pipeline?
response.answer: To train and search hyperparameters for the hybrid SSL+handcrafted pipeline, a moderate compute budget, medium model sizes, a fixed random seed, and experiment tracking with DVC are required.

results.title: How Experiment Management Makes it Easier to Build Better Models
results.content: Developing machine learning models can quickly become a messy, complicated process. As a hobbyist or learner working on a side passion project you often don’t need to worry about tracking or recording your experiments, reproducing results, looking up previous model runs, or collaborating with others. Developing machine learning models at scale for the enterprise is an **iterative, experimental, collaborative process**that can become messy and hard to manage. * An overview of the machine learning model development process. # The machine learning model development process. **Third** is representing the data generating phenomena using statistical and machine learning algorithms by finding a model of best fit. The phenomena by which change anywhere in the machine learning process — especially those changes furthest upstream — will have unanticipated impact on your experiment and results. Having a system for tracking your experiments can help you be more efficient in making the decisions on the data, or the model, or hyperparameters to systematically improve your algorithm’s performance.”. A common saying about machine learning is that it’s when code meets data. When running machine learning experiments, you care about much more than just the code. > What should I be tracking for my machine learning experiments? Finally, compare training metrics across model types and features to verify which types of models have the capacity to learn from the data at all. Once you’re able to find a set of models that are able overfit the training data, you can try regularization approaches to improve the model’s ability to generalize. For your regularization experiments, *investigate the effects of scaling the amount of data on your model.* Track how the training and validation metrics for each model type change as more samples are added to the training set. Once you have a set of hyperparameters that work well with your data, you can fine tune your approach by trying ensembling models together using the top performing models, letting your model train for an extended period of time, or further optimize your feature engineering pipeline. Machine learning is not just when code meets data. It’s when code meets data plus hyperparameters, model architectures, random seeds, compute environments, evaluation metrics, and a whole host of important considerations.

Finally, we set the learning rate, batch size, and the AdamW parameters individually for each model size, leading to compute-optimal scaling that agrees closely with Hoffmann et al. To do so, we conduct a hyperparameter sweep for small-scale models and use the results to fit power laws for the optimal batch size and learning rate as a function of model parameters. discrepancy is the choice of optimization hyperparameters, particularly the batch size: with a fixed batch size of tokens, compute-optimal models at smaller scales train for only a few hundred steps, which is likely too little. Moreover, they report on a small-scale experimental study (with model sizes up to M and training tokens number up to M) in which they observe that a non-decaying learning rate schedule is sufficient for reproducing the Hoffmann et al. Due to limited compute budgets, our hyperparameter sweep only targeted the smaller models in our grid, and furthermore trained each model for only steps, i.e., the optimal point according to the Hoffmann et al. Nevertheless, we observe our final experiment (with parameter tuning) predicts that the optimal (effective) model size at the Chinchilla/Gopher compute scale to be about 16 B parameters larger than the one size predicted using our standard definition.
